steps.body: Fair-cut a bar into b pieces and pick up exactly ONE. That piece is the **unit fraction 1/b** — one piece of a b-cut. Unit fractions are the building blocks of the whole fraction world: everything bigger gets built by stacking them.
Watch one piece shrink as the cut gets finer.

widget.prompt: The bar gets fair-cut into more and more pieces. Slide the cut count until one piece is as SMALL as it can get here.
widget.lowFeedback: One piece is still pretty big — keep cutting finer and watch it shrink.
widget.highFeedback: You've hit the edge of the slider — the finest cut here is 8.
widget.successFeedback: 8 pieces: each is 1/8, the smallest piece on this slider. More pieces from the same bar = smaller pieces. Remember that feeling.

predict.prompt: You'll raise the cut count from 2 pieces up to 8. What happens to the size of ONE piece as the cuts go up?
predict.reveal: More cuts share the SAME bar among more pieces — so every single piece shrinks. Bigger bottom number, smaller piece.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents unit fraction.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for unit fraction must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines unit fraction.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: One piece of a fair 5-cut is 1/5 — the bottom records the cut, the 1 says you hold one piece.
Say it as sharing: five people share a pie fairly, and this is one person's share.

widget.prompt: A pie is fair-cut into 5 pieces. ONE piece is…

commonEntries.feedback: 5/1 is five WHOLE pies! The cut count (5) belongs on the bottom; the single piece rides on top.
The cuts-vs-pieces trap — knife strokes and pieces are different counts. Whatever the knife did, the PIECES number the fraction, and there are five: 1/5.
5/5 is all five pieces — the whole pie. One piece is 1/5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The cut count goes on the bottom; your one piece goes on top.
widget.successFeedback: One of five equal pieces: 1/5. Cut count downstairs, your one piece on top.

steps.body: Writing it down: the bottom number records the cut (b pieces), and the 1 on top says you hold one of them. Meet the unit family: **1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8** — same top, different cuts, very different sizes.

explanationVariants: A unit fraction holds exactly ONE piece — the top must be 1. Only 1/6 qualifies.
Units are the single building blocks; 2/3 is already a stack of two of them.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a UNIT fraction?

options.feedback: One piece of a six-cut — a true unit, top of 1.
That's TWO pieces — a stack of two 1/3 units. A unit fraction holds exactly one.
Six pieces — the whole thing! Units hold a single piece: top number 1.
Zero pieces is an empty hand. A unit fraction holds exactly one piece, no more, no less.

steps.body: Match each cut to its single piece.

widget.prompt: Connect each fair cut to the name of ONE of its pieces.

pairErrors.feedback: A 2-cut makes big pieces — halves. 1/8 comes from the much finer 8-cut.

widget.missFeedback: The bottom number IS the cut count — match each cut to the fraction wearing it downstairs.
widget.successFeedback: Cut of 2 → 1/2, cut of 3 → 1/3, cut of 8 → 1/8. The bottom number reports the cut, every time.

explanationVariants: Two people, two equal shares — each holds one of the two: 1/2.
Sharing among b people always hands each person the unit fraction 1/b.

widget.prompt: Two kids fair-share one granola bar. Each kid's share is…

commonEntries.feedback: Only TWO people share — the bottom counts the shares, and there are 2.
2/1 is two whole bars each! The share count (2) lives downstairs; each kid's single share rides on top.
1/1 is the entire bar for one kid — the other goes hungry. Fair sharing splits it into halves.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two kids share, so the bottom says 2 — each holds one of those shares.
widget.successFeedback: Two equal shares, one each — a half apiece.

hints: The sub was cut so every hiker held exactly one piece — one eighth each.
Three hikers head home and return their pieces to the box.
Count the returned pieces — each is one eighth.
explanationVariants: Each of the 3 returning hikers gives back one 1/8 piece — so 3 eighths sit in the box (and 5 stay with the hikers who remain).
Box + hikers must total all 8 pieces: 3 in the box, 5 out — 3/8 boxed.

widget.prompt: A sub is fair-cut into 8 pieces for 8 hikers — one piece each. Rain sends 3 hikers home before eating, and their pieces go back in the box. How many EIGHTHS are in the box?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 counts the pieces still OUT with the hikers who stayed. The box holds what the 3 leavers returned.
8 would be the whole sub back in the box — but 5 hikers are still out there holding their pieces.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One piece per returning hiker: count the hikers who went home.

takeaways: 1/b is one piece of a fair b-cut — the unit fraction.
The bottom number records the cut; the 1 says you hold one piece.
Finer cuts make smaller units — 1/8 is tiny next to 1/2.
steps.teaser: next: stacking units — how 3/4 is really 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Say the fraction as **sharing**: 1/b is one person's share when b people split something fairly. 1/4? Four people shared; this is one share. The bottom counts the sharers; the top says the piece is yours.

explanationVariants: One of four equal pieces is 1/4 — four shares, you hold one.
Cut count downstairs (4), your single piece on top (1).

widget.prompt: One piece of a fair 4-cut is…

options.feedback: Four shares, one in your hand: 1/4.
4/1 is four wholes — the cut count belongs on the bottom.
That's a piece of a THREE-cut. This bar was cut into four — the bottom says so.
